_readme: Two things: a live test of the current El Nino call in the Andes (Southern Hemisphere season in progress as of August 2026), and a graded review of the 2025-26 Northern Hemisphere season against what this site's La Nina content said. Compiled from published season reports and snowpack surveys, sources listed per section. Redo each year once a season closes.

live_test.title: Live test: the Andes call, right now
live_test.text: This site rates the central Andes as the clearest El Nino beneficiary anywhere, and Portillo as the highest-conviction destination of an El Nino cycle. The 2026 Southern Hemisphere season is the first live test of that call, and it landed. After a slow start that had Portillo still waiting for winter to begin at the start of July, a late-July storm cycle delivered 466 cm in seven days. Portillo reached 611 cm cumulative for the season by 30 July, with 270 cm settled on the Plateau run. Valle Nevado took 157 cm in the week of 22-29 July and opened 44 of its 45 trails with all 13 lifts running, its general manager calling the storms the biggest in decades. Both resorts extended the season into October.
live_test.nuance: The resort-level ranking held up too, not just the regional one. The high central Chilean resorts took the brunt of it, while the Argentine side was far more modest over the same period — Las Lenas sat at an 80 cm base and 230 cm at the summit, and Cerro Catedral reported 30-40 cm of new snow in its upper sectors. That is the split this site predicts: Portillo and Valle Nevado sit where El Nino's frontal systems hit hardest. Worth noting the season was heavily back-loaded, so a July booking made on this call would have looked wrong for weeks before it looked right.

enso_summary: A weak La Nina: ONI bottomed near -0.61 in Oct-Dec 2025, then faded to neutral by Feb-Mar 2026 (-0.21 by JFM). This site would have shown La Nina content through roughly January, then shifted toward neutral for the back half of the season.

headline_wildcard.title: A March heat wave overrode the climate signal across the Interior West
headline_wildcard.text: A prolonged ridge over Utah and the Great Basin produced Colorado's warmest March on record, 3-4F above the previous record, and record March heat across Colorado, Utah and Wyoming. It stripped an already thin snowpack up to 65 days early. Colorado's 1 April snow water equivalent came in at 22% of the 30-year median, against a previous SNOTEL-era low of 9.1 inches in 2012; 2026 managed 3.3 inches. Utah hit 19% of normal, the lowest since records began in 1930 and roughly a fifth of the previous low from 2015. Utah's was a warm-winter problem more than a dry one: mountain precipitation ran near 87% of normal, but warmth turned much of it to rain and pulled peak snowpack forward by more than three weeks. No ENSO-based model, including this one, would have caught it.

regions.predicted: Bullish. La Nina strengthens the Siberian High and the East Asian winter monsoon, the mechanism behind Japan's powder.
regions.actual: Niseko finished at 1,283 cm for the season, over 12 metres. December alone brought 370 cm at village level and 471 cm up top, the biggest December in 20 years. Hakuba took close to 3 metres in December and kept going through March. Rusutsu recorded 992 cm.
regions.note: The strongest clean result of the season. Called bullish, delivered a top-tier year, and the stated mechanism is the one that produced it.

regions.predicted: Bullish, +15-25%. La Nina's top North American beneficiary.
regions.actual: Record December snowfall at Lake Louise, Sunshine, Kicking Horse and Revelstoke, with Silver Star and Sun Peaks past 80% of terrain open by the holidays.
regions.note: Clean on the early season, which is what the published reporting covers well. No comprehensive season-end recap surfaced for BC, so whether the March ridge that wrecked the US Interior West also cut into the Canadian Rockies is unconfirmed.

regions.predicted: Bearish, -15-30%. La Nina shuts off the southern jet corridor.
regions.actual: Record warmth and a persistent lack of wintry precipitation across the Southwest.
regions.note: Correct, though the March ridge means the region underperformed even the bearish call.

regions.predicted: Mixed, slightly favorable. La Nina removes El Nino's suppression of Arctic outbreaks rather than creating a tailwind.
regions.actual: The most impactful winter since 2020-21: a 31-inch storm 23-27 January and a 2-3 foot blizzard 21-23 February. NAO ran negative through December.
regions.note: Right outcome, and for the reason the site now leads with in this region: the NAO did the work, not ENSO. This is the season that prompted making the Northeast NAO-primary.

regions.predicted: Bearish, -10-20%, with an explicit caveat that a few big atmospheric rivers can still rescue the season.
regions.actual: Slow November-December, with only Mt. Rose and Heavenly open and Mammoth at 30% by mid-November. A holiday cycle then delivered 4-6 feet, and a 15-20 February cycle delivered more.
regions.note: The bearish base call was too pessimistic, but the caveat covered what happened. Counting this as partial rather than a hit, because the caveat did the work, not the headline number.

regions.predicted: Mixed / near average. The site explicitly says ENSO has no real predictive power here in any phase.
regions.actual: The worst season on record. Salt Lake City had its least snowy winter ever recorded; Colorado finished at 22% of median April 1 SWE and Utah at 19% of normal.
regions.note: The model correctly refused to credit or blame ENSO here, and the actual driver was exactly what an ENSO model cannot see. But refusing to make a call is not the same as making a good one: a historic collapse happened and this site gave no warning. That is a real limitation, not a technicality.

regions.predicted: Bullish, +15-25%. La Nina's single most reliable US beneficiary.
regions.actual: An active early season, but Washington's 1 April statewide snowpack came in at 52% of normal, in the 5th percentile, after the same record-warm March. A statewide drought emergency was declared on 8 April with every watershed past the drought threshold.
regions.note: The clearest miss of the season. The highest-conviction bullish call on the board, and it finished in the 5th percentile. The mechanism the site relies on here is real, but a warm spring can erase a good winter, and nothing in an ENSO-only framework accounts for that.

regions.predicted: Mixed and elevation-dependent. NAO dominates, not ENSO.
regions.actual: No comprehensive season-end recap found. Scattered reporting describes an active Atlantic storm track with a favourable negative-NAO window in late February.
regions.note: Not enough published data to grade honestly. Left ungraded rather than assigned a flattering verdict.

regions.predicted: n/a for the 2025-26 Northern Hemisphere season.
regions.actual: See the live test above: the 2026 Southern Hemisphere season confirmed the El Nino call.
regions.note: Graded separately in the live test section, under the El Nino phase this site was built to assess.

regions.predicted: n/a for the 2025-26 Northern Hemisphere season.
regions.note: Southern Hemisphere season. Note that Australia is now SAM-primary on this site rather than ENSO-primary, so a future backtest should grade it against SAM.

scorecard.text: Four clean hits, one partial, one clear miss, one case where refusing to make a call was right for the wrong-feeling reason, and one left ungraded for lack of data. The pattern worth taking from it: the calls tracking storm-track position held up, and the calls that failed failed on temperature. Both the Pacific Northwest miss and the Interior West collapse came from warmth, not from storms going to the wrong place.

live_validation.title: What this season changed about the model
live_validation.text: Two things. First, temperature deserves the weight it now carries: the resort scoring added share of season days below freezing as a 30% component precisely because 2025-26 was lost to warmth rather than to a missing storm track. Second, the Northeast result pushed NAO from a footnote to the region's primary driver, and the same logic later moved Australia to SAM. The failures here are the reason the site no longer treats ENSO as the only thing worth reading.

methodology_note: Verdicts are assigned against what this site's content said before the season, not reverse-engineered afterwards. Where published data is thin, the region is marked inconclusive rather than given a generous grade.
